papers.summary: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection from speech benefits from both paralinguistic and linguistic cues, yet model training is frequently constrained by limited data. Fine-tuning a large pretrained speech encoder can easily overfit, while a frozen probe leaves the encoder's task-relevant knowledge underutilized. Therefore, we propose Dual Task Vector Merging, a parameter-efficient method that adapts a frozen wav2vec 2.0 backbone using task knowledge learned outside the AD task. Specifically, we inject two task vectors, derived as weight deltas from emotion- and ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 models, into each transformer layer. During AD training, only layer-wise merging coefficients and a linear classification head are optimized, updating less than 0.1% of the parameters required for full fine-tuning. Speaker-independent experiments on ADReSS and ADReSSo show that dual merging improves over frozen probes, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, in the main binary settings, and gives the best results when combined with LoRA. Evaluation on PROCESS further shows that our advantages transfer to three-class HC/MCI/dementia classification when paired with LoRA. Experiments under reduced training data (20%, 40%, and 80%) confirm reliable gains in low-resource settings.

papers.title: DiPLO: Self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation
papers.authors: Shafeef Omar, Sebastian Sanokowski, Elham Daneshmand, Dian Yu et al.
papers.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner's dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker's execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling 99% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning.

papers.title: Consistency Is the Attack Surface: Detecting Coordinated Retrieval Poisoning with Embedding Geometry
papers.authors: Zeyan Li, Qirong Guo, Jianfeng Xu
papers.summary: Consistency-based defenses for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) rest on an assumption that a sparse adversary breaks: a poisoning campaign may modify a negligible fraction of the corpus, yet retrieval concentrates its passages into the reader's context. Across four Natural Questions retrieval seeds, at least one injection reaches the top-5 in 94.1% of targeted query–seed rows, and all three form a retrieved majority in 52.9%. Under our short-answer protocol, RobustRAG and ReliabilityRAG reach exposure-conditional attack success 0.512, against 0.576 for undefended RAG, while lowering clean accuracy from 0.328 to 0.216. Coordination, however, leaves a fingerprint: a dense, query-anchored component in the evidence embedding geometry. CoordGuard audits this structure from robustly normalized query-weighted affinities, without poison labels, correct answers, or reader gradients. Its always-filter mode suppresses the selected component whenever one forms; a benign-calibrated gate suppresses it only at unusually high scores and traces a robustness–utility frontier. Pooling four retrieval seeds, e5 always-filtering reduces ASRexp to 0.167 overall and 0.138 on parametrically unknown queries, at a 13.6-point clean cost, while a Contriever gate retains clean accuracy 0.315 at ASRexp=0.331. The reduction transfers across two readers, three tasks, and multiple retriever–auditor pairs, and count-matched controls attribute it to component-targeted removal rather than deletion volume. These findings recast poison detection from judging truth to auditing the structure of retrieved evidence.

papers.title: HEL: A Heterogeneous Extensible Layer for GPU-Resident Runtime Orchestration
papers.authors: Agnieszka M. Łupińska, Serban D. Porumbescu, John D. Owens
papers.summary: We describe a GPU-resident runtime system, HEL, built on stateful services that persist throughout the lifespan of a user application. A HEL programmer expresses a workload as an application that spawns coroutine-like tasks, which are then scheduled and run by the HEL runtime. HEL supports synchronous and asynchronous tasks, tasks with runtime dependencies, batched task submission, and automatic retries. Applications and tasks run alongside each other on the spatially partitioned GPU. Using producer-consumer and host-RPC benchmarks together with a PFPL compression case study, we show that HEL demonstrates a performance advantage for underutilized GPUs and for scenarios where HEL enables hiding task latency.

papers.title: Escape Without a Recipe: Maneuver-Agnostic Mars Rover Recovery from Granular Entrapment
papers.authors: Meraj Hossain Promit, Chandak Chakma, Md Jubair Ahmed Sourov, Sejuti Rahman
papers.summary: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z/r = 2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact. A frozen entrapment detector, trained on 81,771 windows spanning three materials and six sinkage levels, supplies a three-state belief to the policy observation. A separate simulator mobility latch gates training rewards. Across five training seeds, mean action evaluation achieves 62.5% escape (range 28.1-81.3%; 32 trials per seed) versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise. A numerical audit identifies a coupling-buffer fault that silently discarded 9.7% of contact nodes at 16 parallel environments. Results establish recovery in the tested simulation regime; physical transfer remains unverified.

papers.title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
papers.authors: Yizheng Xie, Yalda Foroutan, George Shramko, Daniel Rebain et al.
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io

papers.title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning
papers.authors: SeongJun Jeong, Chungwoo Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
papers.summary: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.

papers.title: When Better Policies Leave Harder Failures: Coverage Shift in VLM Success Monitoring
papers.authors: Isabel Guan, Dingyuan Zhang, Shipeng Lyu, I-Ming Chen
papers.summary: Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift: learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.

papers.title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness
papers.authors: Muhammad Waseem, Aakash Ahmad, Pekka Abrahamsson
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.

papers.title: Learning Structured Locomotion References for Optimization-Based Whole-Body Control
papers.authors: Ömer Tarık Banuş, Uluç Saranlı, M. Mert Ankaralı
papers.summary: Quadruped locomotion requires coordinating body motion,contact forces, foothold placement, and gait timing. We present a hierarchical controller in which reinforcement learning adapts these structured locomotion references while a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and whole-body impulse controller retain responsibility for high-frequency execution. The model-based backbone can sustain a nominal trot independently, allowing the policy to focus on when and how to modify an already functional locomotion controller. We train the complete hierarchy in a vectorized controller-in-the-loop environment using a six-direction disturbance curriculum. Under a common simulator and evaluation protocol, the proposed controller achieves 77.29% mean survival across the tested disturbance grid, compared with 50.35% for the model-based reference controller. Training-time channel ablations identify adaptive foothold placement as the largest marginal contributor to grid survival and reveal direction-dependent effects of gait-rate adaptation. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of the proposed hierarchical controller architecture for integrating learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control through structured locomotion references.

papers.title: Finite-Calendar Admission and Deadline-Aware Pruning for UWB Audio
papers.authors: Fengyun Zhang
papers.summary: Isochronous ultra-wideband (UWB) audio transport must deliver a complete service data unit (SDU) before its presentation deadline; fragment reception rate and aggregate throughput do not directly characterize this objective. We formulate admission and online service over a periodic calendar of finite exchange opportunities, explicitly accounting for fragmented SDUs, bounded attempts, calendar alignment, and timing uncertainty. For equal-duration, freely assignable opportunities, an interval-demand condition characterizes finite-job reservation feasibility, and an earliest-deadline-first construction realizes a feasible reservation. A separate necessary capacity bound identifies loads that cannot sustain complete-SDU delivery even with no transmission errors. For online overload control, we study a deadline-aware policy that discards an SDU when its outstanding fragments exceed the remaining eligible opportunities. Across 3,456 replicated scheduling runs and 432 supplemental sensitivity runs, pruning raises eight-stream burst-loss timely completion from 45.441% to 59.399%, a paired difference of 13.958±2.080 percentage points (pointwise 95% interval). At four streams, round robin instead attains slightly higher completion, while heavy overload causes pronounced per-stream imbalance. A finite design enumeration and an evaluated multi-stream fragmentation envelope quantify the interaction among scheduling, payload overhead, and capacity. These findings distinguish provable admission conditions from online deadline salvage and expose the aggregate-throughput versus per-stream-service tradeoff in UWB audio scheduling.

papers.title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
papers.authors: Eman Alashwali, Joud Alraimi, Maryam Almaghrabi
papers.summary: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.

papers.title: ShlokaDhara: A Multi-Speaker Sanskrit Speech Corpus for Learning Meter-Aware Prosody in Text-to-Recitation
papers.authors: Harshal Kausadikar, Onkar Kishor Susladkar, Prathmesh Santosh Choudhari, Vedangi Deepak Deshpande et al.
papers.summary: Sanskrit verse recitation is governed by Chandas, a strict prosodic framework defined by rhythmic Laghu (light) and Guru (heavy) syllables. Because existing Sanskrit speech datasets prioritize ASR or conversational TTS, they lack the metrical fidelity required for authentic verse synthesis. We introduce ShlokaDhara, a 43-hour, multi-speaker Sanskrit speech corpus capturing diverse meters, recitation styles, and melodic variations. We specifically focus on Text-to-Recite, a synthesis task explicitly requiring both prosodic accuracy and metrical correctness. Benchmarking state-of-the-art TTS architectures via an automated UTMOS (neural MOS) predictor demonstrates that XTTS-v2 achieves the highest perceptual quality. We further validate the XTTS-v2 generated samples using two paradigms: subjective assessments by 16 Sanskrit experts and novel empirical metrics, specifically, syllable-level Laghu-Guru duration analysis to objectively quantify structural metrical awareness. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust dataset and evaluation benchmark for prosody-aware computational Sanskrit recitation. Generated Samples: https://shlokadhara.vercel.app/

papers.title: Vibenix: Agentic Software Packaging and Maintenance with Nix
papers.authors: Martim Monis, Martin Schwaighofer, Nuno Saavedra, Alexandra Mendes et al.
papers.summary: Implicit dependencies, uncontrolled network access, and other build-environment impurities create intransparent software supply chains. Identifying every dependency affecting a build is a difficult task. Functional package management addresses this through reproducible packaging, ensuring software relies exclusively on declared, hermetically isolated inputs. However, creating build recipes remains complex and time-consuming, posing a significant barrier to adoption for developers and maintainers. We present Vibenix, an open-source AI-powered agent that bridges this gap by automatically generating Nix packaging expressions. Vibenix uses a large language model (LLM) to iteratively refine recipes through a rule-guided build-repair feedback loop. On 466 packaging tasks from our new NixBench dataset, Vibenix produced buildable packages in 95.3% of cases using Claude Haiku 4.5, compared with 5.6% for a state-of-the-art LLM-based single-shot packaging tool. Manual validation of 100 packages revealed that 47% of the buildable packages were initially functionally correct; a post-build refinement process based on the evaluator-optimizer pattern increased functional correctness by 35 percentage points. On our new NixBench-Repair dataset of package maintenance tasks, Vibenix achieved an 87.6% success rate. These results demonstrate how unreliable LLMs can generate rigorously defined, complete, auditable dependency trees for real-world software, reducing maintainer burden while providing a trustworthy foundation for secure software distribution.

papers.title: SpikeAid: A Streaming Spiking Hearing Aid Framework for Joint Noise Reduction and Wide Dynamic Range Compression
papers.authors: Xiang Hao, Xinyi Chen, Hanwen Liu, Jibin Wu et al.
papers.summary: Modern hearing aids combine noise reduction (NR) with wide dynamic range compression (WDRC) to suppress background interference while compensating for the reduced auditory dynamic range associated with hearing loss. Conventional systems typically process NR and WDRC as separate stages, although the output of NR directly affects the signal levels and envelopes that determine subsequent compression. Recent end-to-end neural approaches can jointly optimize these processes, but their dense computation remains challenging for always-on hearing aids. In this work, we propose SpikeAid, a causal end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) framework for joint NR and WDRC. SpikeAid consists of an NR-Net that constructs complementary speech and noise representations and a WDRC-Net that estimates the corresponding branch gains, with both components jointly optimized according to the final hearing aid objective. To capture the multiscale temporal structures required by joint NR and WDRC in a computationally efficient manner, we further introduce the Delayed Resonate-and-fire Neuron (DRN), which incorporates bio-inspired heterogeneous dendritic delays and resonating dynamics. Experimental results on the hearing aid task show that SpikeAid improves key objective metrics over cascaded processing and outperforms existing spiking speech-processing baselines. Evaluation on the public Intel Neuromorphic Deep Noise Suppression (N-DNS) Challenge further demonstrates state-of-the-art neuromorphic speech-denoising performance with DRN. Finally, we designed an FPGA-based neuromorphic hardware system for efficient deployment of SpikeAid, where it achieves over two orders of magnitude higher energy efficiency than conventional CPU/GPU implementations, demonstrating its potential for energy-efficient hearing aid applications.

papers.title: Lightweight Machine Learning for Classifying Disaster-Related Social Media Posts
papers.authors: Chengjun Jiang, Milena Radenkovic
papers.summary: Classifying disaster-related social-media posts into humanitarian information labels is challenging because individual messages are typically short and context-limited, humanitarian categories can overlap semantically, and the CrisisBench label distribution is strongly imbalanced. This study investigates whether lightweight lexical machine-learning methods can provide effective and computationally efficient classification under these conditions. Using the CrisisBench v1.0 English humanitarian task, comprising 87,455 records across predefined Train, Development and Test splits, we conduct a controlled comparison of TF-IDF representations and lightweight classifiers, with Macro-F1 as the primary model-selection metric. Beyond aggregate predictive performance, the study jointly examines per-label behaviour, directional error patterns, relative decision margins, computational requirements, and the effect of domain-specific training through a tropical-cyclone specialist model. The selected balanced LinearSVC with unigram-bigram TF-IDF and C=0.5 achieved an Accuracy of 0.8282, a Macro-F1 of 0.6578 and a Weighted-F1 of 0.8315 on the held-out Test split. Lower decision margins were substantially associated with prediction errors, while the tropical-cyclone specialist achieved modestly higher in-domain aggregate performance with substantially lower feature and fitting requirements. The study contributes a controlled, label-sensitive and resource-aware evaluation of lightweight humanitarian text classification that characterises not only aggregate performance, but also where these models fail and how their behaviour changes under domain-specific training.

papers.title: Say It or Grab It? Conversational Control of UI Adaptations in Mixed Reality
papers.authors: Sina Elahimanesh, Joao Marcelo Evangelista Belo, Isidora Jeknic, Alexander Koller et al.
papers.summary: Mixed reality interfaces must continuously adapt to a user's changing task and environment, yet adaptation policies are fixed in advance, either preset by the system or configured by the user. Natural language offers a way to state changing needs mid-task, but whether users can express interface behavior this way, and what it gains over direct manipulation, is unknown. We first elicited how users verbalize adaptation needs (N=19). We then built ConverseMR, which translates a spoken request into adaptation objectives and constraints and satisfies them continuously as the user's context changes. In a within-subjects study (N=24), conversational and direct control proved complementary: direct manipulation for precision, ConverseMR for reach and expressive breadth, with their combination rated highest. Spoken commands were rarely final and users frequently refined and replaced them upon experiencing the result, characteristic of, what we call, user-led adaptation, where users communicate adaption needs and the system identifies a solution.

papers.title: A mechanism for TCP-aware Active Queue Management in packet-forwarding devices
papers.authors: Swarnarup Bhunia, Somit Gond, Vayun Goel, Sreelakshmi Manjunath et al.
papers.summary: The deployment of Active Queue Management (AQM) policies is known to be a promising solution to bufferbloat, the problem of persistently-full large buffers in Internet routers. However, most AQMs involve tunable parameters, and some require awareness of the characteristics of the transport-layer protocol implemented at the end systems, thereby rendering their deployment infeasible. We consider one such AQM– a threshold-based queue policy which requires the packet-dropping threshold to be co-designed with relevant TCP parameters. We propose a mechanism that detects network congestion, estimates the congestion window evolution in the end hosts, estimates the required TCP parameter, and produces an optimal value of the packet-dropping threshold. Arguments based on analysis of the TCP fluid model are presented to substantiate the proposed mechanism. A simulation-based performance evaluation reveals the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism, compared to some widely implemented queue policies, in terms of various user- and system-oriented metrics. The proposed mechanism is particularly well-suited for implementation in Software Defined Networks (SDN) where the algorithms can run in the SDN controller and the packet-dropping threshold can be implemented in the data-plane switches through open interfaces.

papers.title: Task Offloading and Resource Allocation for Deterministic Service Provisioning in the IoT-Edge-Cloud Continuum
papers.authors: K. Aghababaiyan, B. Coll-Perales, J. Gozalvez
papers.summary: Future networks will seamlessly integrate computing and communication resources within a unified ecosystem of IoT devices, edge nodes, and cloud servers, forming an IoT-edge-cloud continuum. Within such an ecosystem, tasks can be dynamically offloaded to leverage resources across the continuum and efficiently scale with demand. Task offloading has traditionally focused on minimizing task execution latency or energy consumption. In contrast, we propose a deterministic task offloading and resource allocation scheme for the joint management of communication and computing resources to support services with deterministic service-level requirements. The proposed scheme aims to maximize the number of tasks completed on time, rather than minimizing the latency of individual tasks. To do so, it exploits variable task latency requirements to distribute the workload across the continuum. It can also prioritize high-priority tasks under resource scarcity. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that a deterministic task offloading strategy scales more effectively and can better guarantee timely task completion by balancing resource utilization across the continuum.

papers.title: From Candidate Admission to Task-Level Return: Auditing LLM-Generated Code under Execution Contracts
papers.authors: Hiroyasu Usami, Keisuke Hara, Ayato Tsuboi, Naohiko Matsuda
papers.summary: Admission rules retain generated programs, whereas selection policies return one candidate per task. We audit how these decisions interact with execution contracts in two separately frozen, disjoint HumanEvalPlus cohorts, each comprising 32 tasks, four samples per task per profile and two served profiles. Under the inline execution contract, a structural-and-self-test screen admits 4-9 expanded-suite nonpasses per 80-107 admissions and excludes 14-43 suite passes per 128 planned attempts. A restricted module-supply condition adds 20 and 14 passing admissions for one profile in the respective cohorts, plus one follow-up nonpass, and reduces the excluded suite passes to 14-23. All fixed first-admitted outcomes and abstentions remain unchanged. In the original pool, the added passes enter already all-passing admitted pools; in the follow-up, four of 24 common sample orders lose one passed task. Selected-subset diagnostics separately address registration-sensitive completion and reference-relative assertion disagreement, accounting for input domains and comparator tolerances. In these high-pass pools, candidate retention and task-level return diverge and are reported separately. Results are conditional on the saved pools, contracts and pinned suites; downstream training effects are unmeasured.

papers.title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
papers.authors: Giuseppe Giaimis, Sergei Katkov, Muhammad Azfar Yaqub, Antonio Liotta
papers.summary: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time–accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.

papers.title: Energy-minimized interpolatory B-spline lofting for sequences of closed contours
papers.authors: Shutao Tang, Zixuan Zhao
papers.summary: B-spline lofting through closed cross-sections is common in reverse engineering, but interpolating each section on its own knot vector can produce an unnecessarily large control net. We construct a common-knot method for closed section curves of odd and even degree by minimizing the strain energy of each section subject to its interpolation constraints. Feasibility for closed section data and uniqueness of the resulting saddle-point solution require full row rank of the periodic collocation matrices, a property that a previously proposed periodic Schoenberg-Whitney window condition does not always guarantee. We establish the exact parity distinction: the condition is sufficient at odd point counts but admits singular configurations at every admissible even point count. For the odd and even degrees used here, the natural and shifting anchor knots are nonsingular; at odd point counts the window condition certifies the selected candidate, whereas at even point counts a rank test with an anchor fallback is applied. The lofting method therefore retains a nonsingular square subsystem for each section and uses nestedness to transfer full row rank to the rectangular common-knot system. Across six closed-contour models the common-knot method uses 83-98% fewer control points than traditional interpolating lofting, with section energies no larger than those of a previous knot-selection method within numerical precision.

papers.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
papers.authors: Shihao Weng, Longtian Wang, Yang Feng, Mingfei Cheng et al.
papers.summary: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.

papers.title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
papers.authors: Yunpeng Zhao, Haoxiang Zhang, Chao Liu
papers.summary: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.

papers.title: MOMO: Human Motion from Moving Sounds
papers.authors: Deli Cai, Shuyang Xu, Zhiyang Dou, Zitong Lan et al.
papers.summary: Human responses to sound depend not only on its semantic content, but also on the evolving spatial relationship between source and listener, conveyed through spatial audio and its temporal dynamics. Modeling human reactions to such dynamic spatial audio is important for character animation, human behavior analysis, and robotics. As of yet, existing audio-driven motion generation methods primarily focus on non-spatial or static acoustic conditions, leaving this important problem largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we formulate the novel task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation and introduce two motion-captured datasets. We introduce the Dynamic Spatial Audio and Motion dataset (DySAM) as the first dataset and benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories. Given the importance of dynamic spatial cues of sound sources, we further provide the Dynamic Spatial Audio Localization dataset (DySAL), an auxiliary binaural localization dataset that pairs diverse acoustic events with head poses and moving source trajectories to support spatial audio perception. For benchmarking, we propose MOMO for human Motion generation from Moving Sounds, a diffusion-based framework guided by three coupled principles: localization, understanding, and generation. MOMO performs localization by estimating head-centric spatial direction cues of the moving source directly from raw binaural audio, avoiding reliance on ground-truth source coordinates. It performs understanding by extracting frame-wise audio-content representations, and performs generation by conditioning motion diffusion on both semantic features and dynamic spatial cues. Experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines in motion fidelity, audio-motion alignment, and physical plausibility.

papers.title: StarMind: Challenges and Opportunities in Orbital Computing
papers.authors: Zisheng Gong, Zhaoyu Liu, Houtianfu Wang, O. Tansel Baydas et al.
papers.summary: Space-based artificial intelligence (AI) is moving beyond isolated onboard processing toward constellation-scale computing over optical inter-satellite links (OISLs). Yet current infrastructures remain fragmented, making end-to-end (E2E) coordination across heterogeneous and multi-vendor systems difficult. This article examines the StarMind vision and develops a reference framework for distributed orbital computing. It organizes the system into five layers and defines six standardizable interfaces that link mission intent to resource conditions and trustworthy result delivery. The framework also clarifies the operational constraints that determine whether orbital cooperation is worthwhile. In a representative synthetic aperture radar/interferometric SAR (SAR/InSAR) case study, the framework reduces E2E latency to 41-min, compared with 61-min for localized onboard computing and 146-min for ground-based processing. This gain does not rely on faster processors in orbit. Instead, it comes from reducing contact waiting and urgent Earth downlink traffic through resource-aware task placement and gateway selection. Feasibility analysis shows that the proposed framework is more effective when source datasets are large, output products are compact, and optical inter-satellite link capacity is sufficient. When these conditions are absent, conventional processing may remain preferable. Finally, we discuss research opportunities in joint task partitioning and cross-domain orchestration, hierarchical federated intelligence, and large model-enabled intelligence to advance an interoperable space-ground computing continuum.

papers.title: Semantic Routing Framework for Multi-Domain Telecom Intent-Based Networking
papers.authors: Marwa Tageldien, Bassant Selim, Lokman Sboui
papers.summary: Intent-Based Networking (IBN) is a key enabler of autonomous network management in next-generation networks, as it allows operators to drive the network through high-level intents instead of low-level configuration commands. In this paper, we propose a semantic routing framework for telecom intent classification and translation across the radio access networks (RANs), transport, 5G core, and cloud/edge domains. This framework operates locally to preserve intent privacy and avoid the latency and cost of cloud-based Large Language Model (LLM) solutions. The proposed framework is composed of intent classification and translation. To accurately classify the intent, we propose fine-tuning sentence-transformer models using contrastive learning over a 3GPP TS 28.312-aligned taxonomy of five top-level routes and 22 branches, supported by a telecom-specific codebook of 1,100 intents. In addition, we develop a branchaware, template-driven rule-based module for intent translation that enforces deterministic, hallucination-free parameter extraction and explicit missing-field detection, ensuring a structured and verifiable output pipeline. The numerical results show that the best fine-tuned encoder achieves up to 99.02%/94.61% route/branch classification accuracy, outperforming both base encoders and a commercial embedding baseline. The proposed translator achieves up to 96.24% translation accuracy, compared to 85.37% for a cloud-based LLM benchmark. Moreover, since the proposed pipeline runs entirely on local hardware, an average translation latency of 4.81 ms is recorded against 4,163.58 ms for the cloud-based benchmark, i.e., a speedup of approximately 866x.

papers.title: SENTRY: A Streaming Edge Network Trust Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.authors: Chirantan Banerjee, Soumita Chatterjee, Bhargab B. Bhattacharya, Hafizur Rahaman
papers.summary: Real-time voice cloning has enabled large-scale streaming deepfake and vishing attacks, while existing Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions rely on GPU-based post-processing that requires buffered audio and generalizes poorly to unseen speech synthesis models. This paper presents SENTRY, a hardware-oriented, streaming trust engine for inline deepfake detection at the network edge. SENTRY employs an integer lifting-wavelet front end together with a bank of multiplier-free transforms, including wavelet-packet envelopes, Walsh-Hadamard sequency profiles, waveform micro-statistics, and long-term spectral features, designed so that acoustic analysis needs only integer add, shift, compare and bitwise operations. A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. Under a closed-set protocol, SENTRY reaches 98.75% accuracy at a 1.25% equal-error rate (EER) on WaveFake, with perfect separation of HiFi-GAN and WaveGlow; its supervised track alone achieves an AUC of 0.9994 (fused: 0.9993). On ASVspoof 2019 LA (attacks A01-A06) over an 8 kHz mu-law telephony channel, it reaches 94.75% accuracy at a 5.05% EER, with a supervised-track AUC of 0.9948 (fused: 0.9884) and per-attack EERs below 7%. In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready. These results indicate that deepfake screening can be placed inline without GPUs or floating-point hardware; generalization to unseen generators is left to future work.

papers.title: SLIM: Learning an Operator for Material-Efficient 3D Lattice Refinement
papers.authors: Yueze Zhu, Yu Xing, Tianyang Xue, Peng-Shuai Wang et al.
papers.summary: Lattice inverse-design methods can generate cells that match prescribed effective properties, but property feasibility does not imply material efficiency. Removing redundant material from an existing lattice while preserving its homogenized elasticity ordinarily requires solving a separate constrained topology optimization problem for each cell, making large-scale refinement computationally expensive. We introduce SLIM (Structural Lightweighting via Implicit Mapping), a neural lattice-refinement model that replaces this per-instance iterative optimization with a single forward prediction. SLIM uses a dual-octree implicit network to predict the signed-distance field of a lightweight lattice and is trained on input–output pairs generated by property-constrained topology optimization. To improve stiffness preservation, we use homogenization sensitivities computed on the optimized target to estimate how residual voxel errors in a prediction affect its homogenized stiffness, and penalize this estimated change during training. Once trained, SLIM requires no topology optimization, homogenization analysis, or sensitivity evaluation during prediction. On the held-out test set of 906 lattices, SLIM achieves a mean relative volume-fraction reduction of 15.90%, a lightweighting success rate of 90.51%, and a mean normalized aggregate TO-target error of 0.636%, while reducing the average per-lattice generation time from 2516.0 s with direct TO to approximately 0.5 s. These results show that SLIM provides a fast neural surrogate for repeated topology-optimization-based refinement of 3D lattices.

papers.title: Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: A Case Study of GPT-6 Astra
papers.authors: Qiang Zou, Jiajun Shen, Zhijie Yang, Yuhao Wang et al.
papers.summary: Recent advances in general-purpose AI models and agentic systems have enabled them to perform some CAD tasks. A systematic assessment is now needed to establish what these systems can accomplish and how well their outputs meet engineering requirements. This paper presents an empirical study of GPT-6 Astra, a SOTA general-purpose AI model, across four basic CAD tasks: model understanding, generation, editing, and evaluation. We design test cases spanning different levels of complexity and engineering requirements. The results show that GPT-6 Astra can support multiple stages of CAD workflows, with successful outcomes in cases involving nontrivial geometric complexity. This suggests that general-purpose AI is beginning to offer practical value in almost all steps in CAD workflow. However, gaps remain between generating visually plausible geometry and producing valid, functional, and editable CAD models. Recurring errors in freeform geometry, parameter dependencies, and mating relationships between parts limit engineering usefulness. Agentic iterative refinement can improve results but does not consistently resolve critical errors; long completion times further constrain practical use.

papers.title: From Neglect to Resignation: Understanding the Evolution of Mobile Privacy
papers.authors: Yibo Meng, Ziqi Liu, Lionel Z. Wang, Shuning Zhang et al.
papers.summary: This decade-long longitudinal qualitative study follows 31 smartphone users in China across four interview waves (2014-2023) to examine how mobile privacy understanding evolves alongside shifting computing infrastructures. Findings reveal three stages shaped by distinct interactional mechanisms: early functional acceptance of permission-based data access, growing vigilance triggered by behavioral tracking feedback loops, and eventual resignation as AI-driven inference made ecosystem-level profiling feel inescapable. Rather than a stable attitude, digital resignation emerges through cumulative infrastructure exposure, as each new system layer retroactively reinterpreted earlier permissions and exhausted users' capacity for self-management. The study challenges permission-centric design assumptions and proposes inference visibility, context isolation, and automated privacy agency as system-level responses.

papers.title: GazeAgent: VLM-Guided Implicit Gaze Calibration from Egocentric Multimodal Behavior for AI Glasses
papers.authors: Yuhong Zhang, Khanh An Nguyen, Xinyu Tian, KungYi Chang et al.
papers.summary: AI glasses typically require explicit, user-specific eye-tracker calibration, and accuracy can drift when the device shifts during use. We present GazeAgent, a VLM-guided framework that continuously and adaptively improves gaze-calibration accuracy from naturally occurring behavior without asking users to interrupt their activities. GazeAgent identifies precise visual attention (PVA) events from multimodal streams of inertial measurement unit (IMU), gaze, and wearer-hand signals, validates their task relevance, and localizes functional targets as pseudo-calibration targets. In a 10-participant scripted study, the system detected all 820 predefined PVA opportunities and, under device disturbance, reduced median gaze error by 44.1% compared with explicit calibration. In a five-participant case study, autonomous calibration produced the lowest workload and interruption ratings, and all participants preferred it for routine use. By deriving task-critical targets from natural multimodal behavior, GazeAgent demonstrates the potential for continuous, adaptive, and low-burden gaze interaction on egocentric AI glasses.
